source: Posner and Saran (2025) Judge AI: Assessing Large Language Models in Judicial Decision-Making
finding: GPT-4o was run on the 2x2 war-crimes appeal (sympathy x precedent consistency) first used on federal judges. It followed precedent and ignored sympathy, like the law students and unlike the judges. Prompt engineering toward realism mostly failed.
numbers: Original: 31 US federal judges. 2x2 design. One model (GPT-4o). Abstract page only; no cell counts on the page.
quote: The authors conclude that Judge AI is a formalist judge, not a human judge.
limits: Abstract page only, not the full paper. One model. Closes gap 4 in direction, not in effect size.
agent_relevance: An LLM judge is a formalist. Sympathy cues did not pull it off a precedent, so outcome-bias is less of a risk in this setting, but the model may also fail to see when a precedent should be distinguished.

source: Tech.co report on Posner and Saran (2025)
finding: Press numbers for the same study: judges swayed by sympathy; students stuck to precedent; GPT followed precedent in over 90% of cases even with sympathetic defendants. Prompts that taught legal realism or asked for justice beyond the law did not change this.
numbers: Judges swayed by sympathy 65% of the time; students followed precedent 85% overall; GPT over 90%.
limits: Secondary source. No sample sizes. Figures not checked against the paper.
agent_relevance: Shows stability across at least three prompt framings on this one task (gap 3 only partly, and not for abstention).

source: Posner and Saran (2026) Silicon Formalism: Rules, Standards, and Judge AI (as reported by The Register)
finding: On a choice-of-law car accident task given to 61 federal judges, newer models applied the legally correct rule far more often than judges. Weaker or smaller models did not. No sympathy effect for GPT.
numbers: Law-following rate: GPT-5 100%, Gemini 3 Pro 100%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 92%, o4-mini 79%, Llama 4 Maverick 75%, Llama 4 Scout 50%, GPT-4.1 50%, human judges 52%.
limits: Press write-up, not the paper. Trials per model and prompts unknown. A rule-application task, not an analogy task. Where the doctrine is a standard, judges have discretion.
agent_relevance: Spread across models (50 to 100%) means precedent-following is a model property to measure, not assume. Test our scaffold on a weak model.

source: University of Chicago News (2026) How do AI judges compare to human ones
finding: Describes the same studies. Judges gave inconsistent outcomes and some errors in choice-of-law. Models applied rules consistently. Students apply law as rigidly as AI.
numbers: No sample sizes or model names on the page.

source: Braman and Nelson (2007) Mechanism of motivated reasoning? Analogical perception in discrimination disputes, AJPS 51(4)
finding: Two experiments with a mock news article and an embedded precedent. People judged precedents whose outcome fit their policy views as more analogous. The bias was strongest for moderately similar cases. Law students differed from laypeople, but legal training did not remove the bias.
numbers: Two experiments; Exp 1 undergraduates, Exp 2 undergraduates plus law students. Per-condition means, N and effect sizes are NOT on the page (gap 5 stays open on exact numbers).
limits: Abstract-level only. Exact effect size and N not retrieved; the book chapter PDF was blocked (403).
agent_relevance: Selection of an analogue is outcome-driven when similarity is ambiguous. Hide the outcome while ranking analogues for mid-similarity cases.

source: Schauer (HKS working paper) Why precedent in law (and elsewhere) is not totally (or even substantially) about analogy
finding: Precedent is binding even when the decider disagrees; analogy is a free choice of the most useful analogue. They are different kinds of constraint.
numbers: No numbers. The page summary does not mention Sunstein, so gap 9 is not closed.
agent_relevance: Our agent should separate two moves: a binding rule from a past ruling (follow) versus an analogue as a heuristic (choose). Different operators.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Evaluating the Robustness of Analogical Reasoning in LLMs (full HTML)
finding: Tested GPT-3, 3.5, 4 on counterfactual variants of Webb et al. tasks. No reasoning-trained model or chain-of-thought was tested, so gap 10 is not answered by this paper.
numbers: Letter-string zero-generalisation pooled: humans 0.754, GPT-3 0.488, GPT-3.5 0.350, GPT-4 0.452. Digit matrices original vs alt-blank: humans 0.715 vs 0.771; GPT-3.5 0.813 vs 0.480; GPT-4 0.810 vs 0.477. Stories GPT-4 original 0.86 (31/36), paraphrase 0.72 (26/36); humans 0.78 (564/720) and 0.70 (503/720). Human N 263, 301, 245.
limits: 2023-era models only. Authors state they did not test reasoning-trained models. Story set small (36 items). The HTML read covered the first 100,000 of about 105,000 characters.
agent_relevance: Analogy by LLMs breaks under counterfactual stimuli; test a scaffold step on perturbed items, not only on the original benchmark.

source: Hodel and West (2024) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Failed to replicate zero-shot letter-string analogy: GPT-3 struggled on simple modified versions while humans stayed high. Argues contamination is not ruled out.
numbers: Abstract only; no accuracy figures retrieved. v1 Aug 2023, v2 May 2024.
quote: Zero-shot reasoning is an extraordinary claim that requires extraordinary evidence.
agent_relevance: Same lesson: test with counterfactual items.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Reasoning or Reciting? Exploring the capabilities of LMs through counterfactual tasks, NAACL
finding: On 11 tasks with counterfactual variants, models do better than chance but performance drops substantially and consistently from default conditions.
numbers: 11 tasks. No scores on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract only; 2023-era models. Does not itself test reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Supports building rule-changed checks for analogy steps.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners, ICLR (analogical prompting)
finding: The model writes its own relevant examples (and optionally knowledge) before solving. Beats 0-shot CoT and manual few-shot CoT on most tasks. Closest tested analogue to analogue retrieval in a non-legal task with exact labels, but it has no isolated 'name the rule the analogue stands for' arm, so gap 1 is only partly addressed.
numbers: GSM8K GPT-3.5: 0-shot CoT 75.8, 5-shot CoT 76.7, analogical 77.8. MATH GPT-3.5: 33.9, 34.9, 37.3. PaLM2 GSM8K 78.2, 80.7, 81.7. Codeforces GPT-3.5 Acc@1: 0-shot CoT 9, 3-shot CoT 11, exemplars 13, knowledge+exemplars 15. BIG-Bench word sorting 67.6, 68.4, 75.2.
limits: Gains are 1-3 points on math, probably inside noise for small test sets; no token-matched arm (generating exemplars costs tokens). Last 24,500 characters of the page not read.
agent_relevance: Self-generated analogues are cheap with small gain. A rule-naming step is plausible but unproven.

finding: Diverse exemplars beat non-diverse ones. Number of exemplars saturates at about 3. Self-consistency stacks on top.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K/MATH: K=1 76.1/34.8; K=3 77.5/37.3; K=5 77.8/37.1. Non-diverse 75.9/35.2 vs diverse 77.8/37.3. With self-consistency 85.3/46.0.
limits: Single model family; self-consistency adds tokens, so not an equal-token comparison.
agent_relevance: Retrieve about 3 analogues with varied features, not many near-duplicates. This fits the legal point that likeness should span relevant features.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Case-Based or Rule-Based: How Do Transformers Do the Math?
finding: Transformers rely on case-based matching, not rules, in addition. Rule-Following Fine-Tuning (rules in input, model recites and applies them step by step) generalises far beyond the training range. A direct test of 'rule beats nearest case' (gap 7), but by fine-tuning.
numbers: GPT-3.5 trained on 1-5 digit addition reaches over 95% at 12 digits from 100 samples, over 40 points above scratchpad. Llama-2-7B RFFT about 91.1% at 9 digits vs scratchpad under 40%. Untrained GPT-3.5 direct answer 46.2% at 15 digits. Leave-square-out: Llama-2-7B from scratch 30.2% on held-out square vs 92% random split.
limits: Fine-tuning, arithmetic, not prompting, not legal. Per-length tables only in figures. Last 44,000 characters not read.
agent_relevance: An explicit rule in context beats case matching out of distribution. Supports Levi's step 2 (state the rule) as an operator, to be tested in prompting.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) legal analogy benchmark 2510.08710, re-read for gaps 2, 3 and 8
finding: Task 3 (significance and distinction judged with a factor hierarchy DAG) stays low. The paper does not test code-side hierarchy lookup, does not discuss precedent era, and has no typed fallback for no-analogue cases.
numbers: Task 3 accuracy: gemini-flash 11.46, gemini-pro 21.74, gpt-oss-120b 22.53, gpt-5 23.32, qwen3-thinking 33.99, qwen3-non-thinking 0.00.
limits: Gaps 2, 3 and 8 are not answered. One run per cell. Read through a page summariser.
agent_relevance: The hierarchy is the solver's ground truth. Giving that lookup to the agent as a tool is the obvious test, still undone.

source: Zhang, Gray et al. (2025) 2506.00694 abstention table re-read
finding: The two garbled abstention values now read cleanly from the HTML table: Llama-3-70B 3.33%, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B 23.33%. Test 3 has 30 triples per mode. One prompt per model; no alternative prompts. The two abstention phrases in the paper differ (Sec 4.2 vs Appendix A).
numbers: Abstention Test 3: GPT-4o 86.67, Qwen-QWQ-32B 56.67, Maverick 50.00, R1-Distill 23.33, Llama-3-70B 3.33, Llama-3-8B/Scout/4o-mini 0.00. N=30 per model.
limits: Table read through a page summariser, not the PDF. Prompt stability (gap 3) NOT tested. Era effect (gap 8) absent: synthetic triples with no dates.
agent_relevance: Abstention varies 0 to 87% on 30 items with one prompt: treat as unstable until prompt variants are run. Prefer a typed 'no analogue' output checked in code over a free-text refusal.

source: Zhang, Savelka, Ashley (2025) 2510.20941 re-read for unknown option
finding: The only abstention route is an 'unknown' answer in Tasks 2-3. No typed fallback and no prompt variants. Weak models use 'unknown' heavily instead of answering.
numbers: n=236. Task 2 GPT-5 75.42% (178/236), 3 unknown (1.27%), 55 false negatives. Gemini-Pro 42.37% (100/236) with 131 unknown (about 55.5%). Gemini-Flash 6.36%. Task 3 (answer always false): GPT-5 and Gemini-Pro 100%, Qwen3 97.46%, Flash-Lite 91.95%, Flash 62.71%.
limits: Single prompt per task. Unknown may stand in for a fallback; not tested as one. Note: the earlier critique gave 73.31% (173/236) for another cell; GPT-5 Task 2 is 75.42% here.
agent_relevance: G6 abstention can look like accuracy loss: Gemini-Pro lost about half its Task 2 score to unknowns. Score abstentions separately from errors.

source: Katz and Zamir (2026) LLMs and human judges on about 50,000 vignette decisions (search summary only)
finding: Search summary says GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4 and Gemini 2.5 Flash are more formalist than humans; asking them to consider sympathy or predict judges reduces formalism somewhat. Not opened (page was a bot check).
agent_relevance: If true, formalism is general across models and prompt framing shifts it only a little.

source: SAGE 2026 LLM rerun of Spamann and Klohn (search summary only)
finding: Search summary says an LLM rerun behaved like students, not judges. Page was a firewall interstitial, so the paper was not read.
limits: Not opened; authors and numbers unknown. Possibly the same finding as d01.
